Introduction

Mock ϑ\vartheta-functions

Early in 1920, three months before his death, S. Ramanujan wrote his last letter to G.H. Hardy. For the mathematical part of this letter see [21, pp. 127–131] (also reproduced in [4]). In the course of it he said: “I discovered very interesting functions recently which I call ‘Mock’ ϑ\vartheta-functions. Unlike the ‘False’ ϑ\vartheta-functions (studied partially by Prof. Rogers in his interesting paper [22]) they enter into mathematics as beautifully as the ordinary ϑ\vartheta-functions. I am sending you with this letter some examples.” He then provided a long list of mock ϑ\vartheta-functions, together with identities satisfied by them. The first three pages in which Ramanujan explained what he meant by a mock ϑ\vartheta-function are very obscure.

G.N. Watson wrote the first papers ([26] and [27]) to elucidate the mock ϑ\vartheta-functions. The first of these is Watson’s Presidential Address to the London Mathematical Society in 1935. He entitled it “The Final Problem: An Account of the Mock Theta Functions.” In it he writes: “I make no apologies for my subject being what is now regarded as old-fashioned, because, as a friend remarked to me a few months ago, I am an old-fashioned mathematician.” His methods may have been a bit old-fashioned, but looking at the number of articles on mock ϑ\vartheta-functions that have appeared since 1935, or even in the last ten years, we must conclude that the subject is still up-to-date.

In these two papers, Watson proves most of the assertions found in the letter of Ramanujan. The first paper considers only the third-order functions. It provides three new mock ϑ\vartheta-functions not mentioned in the letter. The bulk of the paper is devoted to the modular transformation properties of these functions. To get these transformations, he first proves certain identities. For example, for the third order mock ϑ\vartheta-function

f⁡(q):=1+q(1+q)2+q4(1+q)2​(1+q2)2+q9(1+q)2​(1+q2)2​(1+q3)2+⋯f(q):=1+\frac{q}{(1+q)^{2}}+\frac{q^{4}}{(1+q)^{2}(1+q^{2})^{2}}+\frac{q^{9}}{(1+q)^{2}(1+q^{2})^{2}(1+q^{3})^{2}}+\cdots

he finds:

f⁡(q)=2(q)∞​∑n∈𝐙(−1)n​q32​n2+12​n1+qn,f(q)=\frac{2}{(q)_{\infty}}\sum_{n\in\mathbf{Z}}\frac{(-1)^{n}q^{\frac{3}{2}n^{2}+\frac{1}{2}n}}{1+q^{n}}, (1)

with q=e2​π​i​τq=e^{2\pi i\tau}, τ∈ℋ:={τ∈𝐂∣Im⁡(τ)>0}\tau\in\mathcal{H}:=\{\tau\in\mathbf{C}\mid\operatorname{Im}(\tau)>0\}, and (q)∞=∏n=1∞(1−qn)=q−124​η​(τ)(q)_{\infty}=\prod_{n=1}^{\infty}(1-q^{n})=q^{-\frac{1}{24}}\eta(\tau), where η\eta is the Dedekind eta-function.

In Watson’s second paper on mock ϑ\vartheta-functions, he moves on to the fifth order functions. He manages to prove all of the identities given by Ramanujan in his letter. However, he is unable to find the modular transformation properties, simply because he is unable to find identities like (1) for the fifth order functions. He even expressed his doubts about finding anything comparable to (1). However Andrews (see [2]) was able to find comparable results for most of the fifth order functions. For example, for the fifth order function which Watson denotes by f0f_{0} one finds

f0​(q)=1(q)∞​∑n≥0∑|j|≤n(−1)j​q52​n2+12​n−j2​(1−q4​n+2),f_{0}(q)=\frac{1}{(q)_{\infty}}\sum_{n\geq 0}\sum_{|j|\leq n}(-1)^{j}q^{\frac{5}{2}n^{2}+\frac{1}{2}n-j^{2}}(1-q^{4n+2}),

which may be rewritten as

f0(q)=1(q)∞(∑n+j≥0,n−j≥0−∑n+j<0,n−j<0)(−1)jq52​n2+12​n−j2.f_{0}(q)=\frac{1}{(q)_{\infty}}\left(\sum_{n+j\geq 0,n-j\geq 0}-\sum_{n+j<0,n-j<0}\right)(-1)^{j}q^{\frac{5}{2}n^{2}+\frac{1}{2}n-j^{2}}. (2)

The seventh order functions were mostly neglected by Watson, perhaps because Ramanujan makes no positive assertions about them. However A. Selberg (see [23]) provides a full account of the behaviour of the seventh order functions near the unit circle. In [12, pp. 666] we find identities similar to (2) for the seventh order mock ϑ\vartheta-functions ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0}, ℱ1\mathcal{F}_{1} and ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2}. For example (slightly rewritten)

ℱ0(q)=1(q)∞(∑r,s≥0−∑r,s<0)(−1)r+sq32​r2+4​r​s+32​s2+12​r+12​s.\mathcal{F}_{0}(q)=\frac{1}{(q)_{\infty}}\left(\sum_{r,s\geq 0}-\sum_{r,s<0}\right)(-1)^{r+s}q^{\frac{3}{2}r^{2}+4rs+\frac{3}{2}s^{2}+\frac{1}{2}r+\frac{1}{2}s}. (3)

In [11] L. Göttsche and D. Zagier consider sums like the ones in (2) and (3). They call them theta-functions for indefinite lattices. For some special cases they find modular transformation properties for these functions. However, these results do not include the sums in (2) and (3). In [20], a theorem about the modularity of a certain family of qq-series associated with indefinite binary quadratic forms is given. Again, the results do not include the sums in (2) and (3).

This thesis

This thesis is the result of my research on the following two questions, both posed by Don Zagier:

  1. 1.

    How do the mock ϑ\vartheta-functions fit in the theory of modular forms?

  2. 2.

    Is there a theory of indefinite theta functions?

Since most of the mock ϑ\vartheta-functions had been related to sums like the one in (1), I first considered this type of sum. The result of this research is Chapter 1. In it we consider the series

∑n∈𝐙(−1)n​eπ​i​(n2+n)​τ+2​π​i​n​v1−e2​π​i​n​τ+2​π​i​u(τ∈ℋ,v∈𝐂,u∈𝐂∖(𝐙​τ+𝐙)).\sum_{n\in\mathbf{Z}}\frac{(-1)^{n}e^{\pi i(n^{2}+n)\tau+2\pi inv}}{1-e^{2\pi in\tau+2\pi iu}}\qquad(\tau\in\mathcal{H},v\in\mathbf{C},u\in\mathbf{C}\setminus(\mathbf{Z}\tau+\mathbf{Z})).

This function was also studied by Lerch in [15] (see [14] for an abstract). Therefore we call this a Lerch sum. This sum is of the same type as the sum in (1). The function does not transform like a Jacobi form. However, we find that on addition of a (relatively easy) correction term the function does transform like a Jacobi form. This correction term is real-analytic.

In Chapter 2 we consider certain indefinite ϑ\vartheta-functions, in an attempt to give a partial answer to the second question. These indefinite ϑ\vartheta-functions are modified versions of the sums considered by Göttsche and Zagier in [11]. We find elliptic and modular transformation properties for these functions. Because of the modifications the indefinite ϑ\vartheta-functions are no longer holomorphic (in general). Although the results in this chapter are more general than the results in [11], the second question is far from being solved. This is because we only consider indefinite quadratic forms of type (r−1,1)(r-1,1). It remains a problem of considerable interest to develop a theory of theta-series for quadratic forms of arbitrary type.

In [3] Andrews gives most of the fifth order mock theta functions as Fourier coefficients of meromorphic Jacobi forms, namely certain quotients of ordinary Jacobi theta-series. This is the motivation for the study of the modularity of Fourier coefficients of meromorphic Jacobi forms, in Chapter 3. We find that modularity follows on adding a real-analytic correction term to the Fourier coefficients.

In Chapter 4 we use the results from Chapter 2, together with (2), (3) and similar identities for other mock ϑ\vartheta-functions, to get the modular transformation properties of the seventh-order mock ϑ\vartheta-functions and most of the fifth-order functions. The final result is that we can write each of these mock ϑ\vartheta-functions as the sum of two functions HH and GG, where:

  • •

    HH is a real-analytic modular form of weight 1/2 and is an eigenfunction of the appropriate Casimir operator with eigenvalue 3/16 (this is also the eigenvalue of holomorphic modular forms of this weight; for the theory of real-analytic modular forms see for example [16, Ch. IV]); and

  • •

    GG is a theta series associated to a negative definite unary quadratic form, i.e. has the form ∑sgn⁡(f)​β​(2​f2​y)​e−π​i​f2​τ−2​π​i​f​b\sum\operatorname{sgn}(f)\beta(2f^{2}y)e^{-\pi if^{2}\tau-2\pi ifb}, where ff ranges over a certain arithmetic progression a​𝐙+ba\mathbf{Z}+b (a,b∈𝐐a,b\in\mathbf{Q}), τ=x+i​y∈ℋ\tau=x+iy\in\mathcal{H} and β⁡(x)=∫x∞u−12​e−π​u​𝑑u\beta(x)=\int_{x}^{\infty}u^{-\frac{1}{2}}e^{-\pi u}du. Moreover GG is bounded as τ\tau tends vertically to any rational limit.

This decomposition is thus similar to the one found in [29] for an Eisenstein series of weight 3/2, the holomorphic part of the series, in that case, having class numbers as Fourier coefficients.

Many of the results of Chapter 4 could also be deduced using the methods from Chapter 1 or Chapter 3 instead of Chapter 2, i.e. we have actually given 3 approaches to proving modularity properties of the mock ϑ\vartheta-functions.

Chapter 1 Lerch Sums

1 Introduction

In this chapter, we first study a function hh, which is essentially the function φ\varphi studied by Mordell in [17] and [18]. We reproduce some of the results of Mordell. In the next section we study a function μ\mu, which is essentially a function studied by Lerch in [15]. We find elliptic and modular transformation properties of this function. One of these transformations involves the function hh:

1−i​τ​eπ​i​(u−v)2/τ​μ​(uτ,vτ,−1τ)+μ⁡(u,v,τ)=12​i​h​(u−v,τ).\frac{1}{\sqrt{-i\tau}}\ e^{\pi i(u-v)^{2}/\tau}\mu\Bigl(\frac{u}{\tau},\frac{v}{\tau};-\frac{1}{\tau}\Bigr)+\mu(u,v;\tau)=\frac{1}{2i}h(u-v;\tau).

In section 4 we find a real-analytic function RR with essentially the same elliptic and modular transformation properties as μ\mu. Combining the properties of μ\mu and RR we find a real-analytic function μ~\tilde{\mu}, which transforms like a Jacobi form.

In the last section we relate hh to a period integral of a unary theta function of weight 3/2.

2 The Mordell integral

In this section, we present results of Mordell found in [17] and [18], in a form suitable for the purpose of this chapter. The function hh defined in Definition 1.1 is essentially the function φ\varphi studied by Mordell: φ(x;τ)=−12τe−πiτ/4+πixh(x−τ2+12;τ)\varphi(x;\tau)=-\frac{1}{2}\tau e^{-\pi i\tau/4+\pi ix}h(x-\frac{\tau}{2}+\frac{1}{2};\tau). The same function was used earlier by Riemann (as described by Siegel [24]) to prove the functional equation for the Riemann zeta function. Mordell was the first to analyze the behaviour of this integral relative to modular transformations. Consequently, we shall refer to this integral as the Mordell integral.

Definition 1.1

For z∈𝐂z\in\mathbf{C} and τ∈ℋ\tau\in\mathcal{H} set

h⁡(z)=h⁡(z,τ):=∫𝐑eπ​i​τ​x2−2​π​z​xcosh⁡π​x​𝑑x.h(z)=h(z;\tau):=\int_{\mathbf{R}}\frac{e^{\pi i\tau x^{2}-2\pi zx}}{\cosh\pi x}\,dx.

The function hh has the following properties:

h⁡(z)+h⁡(z+1)=2−i​τ​eπ​i​(z+12)2/τh(z)+h(z+1)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{-i\tau}}\,e^{\pi i(z+\frac{1}{2})^{2}/\tau},

(2)

h⁡(z)+e−2​π​i​z−π​i​τ​h​(z+τ)=2​e−π​i​z−π​i​τ/4h(z)+e^{-2\pi iz-\pi i\tau}h(z+\tau)=2e^{-\pi iz-\pi i\tau/4},

z↦h⁡(z,τ)z\mapsto h(z;\tau) is the unique holomorphic function satisfying (1) and (2),

(4)

hh is an even function of zz,

(5)

h(zτ;−1τ)=−i​τe−πiz2/τh(z;τ)h(\frac{z}{\tau};-\frac{1}{\tau})=\sqrt{-i\tau}\,e^{-\pi iz^{2}/\tau}\,h(z;\tau),

(6)

h⁡(z,τ)=eπ​i4​h​(z,τ+1)+e−π​i4​eπ​i​z2/(τ+1)τ+1​h​(zτ+1,ττ+1)\displaystyle{h(z;\tau)=e^{\frac{\pi i}{4}}h(z;\tau+1)+e^{-\frac{\pi i}{4}}\frac{e^{\pi iz^{2}/(\tau+1)}}{\sqrt{\tau+1}}\ h\Bigl(\frac{z}{\tau+1};\frac{\tau}{\tau+1}\Bigr)}.

Proof.

(1) We have

h⁡(z)+h⁡(z+1)=∫𝐑eπ​i​τ​x2−2​π​z​xcosh⁡π​x​(1+e−2​π​x)​𝑑x=2​∫𝐑eπ​i​τ​x2−2​π​x​(z+12)​𝑑x.h(z)+h(z+1)=\int_{\mathbf{R}}\frac{e^{\pi i\tau x^{2}-2\pi zx}}{\cosh\pi x}(1+e^{-2\pi x})\,dx=2\int_{\mathbf{R}}e^{\pi i\tau x^{2}-2\pi x(z+\frac{1}{2})}\,dx.

3 Lerch sums

In this section we will study the function

∑n∈𝐙(−1)n​eπ​i​(n2+n)​τ+2​π​i​n​v1−e2​π​i​n​τ+2​π​i​u(τ∈ℋ,v∈𝐂,u∈𝐂∖(𝐙​τ+𝐙)).\sum_{n\in\mathbf{Z}}\frac{(-1)^{n}e^{\pi i(n^{2}+n)\tau+2\pi inv}}{1-e^{2\pi in\tau+2\pi iu}}\qquad(\tau\in\mathcal{H},v\in\mathbf{C},u\in\mathbf{C}\setminus(\mathbf{Z}\tau+\mathbf{Z})).

This function was also studied by Lerch. The original paper [15] is in Czech and is not very easy to obtain. See [14] for an abstract in German. We will prove elliptic and modular transformation properties of this function in Proposition 1.4 and 1.5 respectively. These results are equivalent to the results found by Lerch.

It is more convenient to normalize the above sum by dividing by the classical Jacobi theta function ϑ\vartheta. (Lerch did this too.) We will first give, without proof, some standard properties of ϑ\vartheta. For the theory of ϑ\vartheta-functions see [19].

Proposition 1.3

For z∈𝐂z\in\mathbf{C} and τ∈ℋ\tau\in\mathcal{H} define

ϑ⁡(z)=ϑ⁡(z,τ):=∑ν∈12+𝐙eπ​i​ν2​τ+2​π​i​ν​(z+12).\vartheta(z)=\vartheta(z;\tau):=\sum_{\nu\in\frac{1}{2}+\mathbf{Z}}e^{\pi i\nu^{2}\tau+2\pi i\nu(z+\frac{1}{2})}.

(3)

Up to a multiplicative constant, z↦ϑ⁡(z)z\mapsto\vartheta(z) is the unique holomorphic function satisfying (1) and (2).

(4)

ϑ⁡(−z)=−ϑ⁡(z)\vartheta(-z)=-\vartheta(z).

(5)

The zeros of ϑ\vartheta are the points z=n​τ+mz=n\tau+m, with n,m∈𝐙n,m\in\mathbf{Z}. These are simple zeros.

(6)

ϑ⁡(z,τ+1)=eπ​i4​ϑ​(z,τ)\vartheta(z;\tau+1)=e^{\frac{\pi i}{4}}\vartheta(z;\tau).

(7)

ϑ⁡(zτ,−1τ)=−i​−i​τ​eπ​i​z2/τ​ϑ​(z,τ)\vartheta(\frac{z}{\tau};-\frac{1}{\tau})=-i\sqrt{-i\tau}e^{\pi iz^{2}/\tau}\vartheta(z;\tau).

(8)

ϑ(z;τ)=−iq18ζ−12∏n=1∞(1−qn)(1−ζqn−1)(1−ζ−1qn)\displaystyle{\vartheta(z;\tau)=-iq^{\frac{1}{8}}\zeta^{-\frac{1}{2}}\prod_{n=1}^{\infty}(1-q^{n})(1-\zeta q^{n-1})(1-\zeta^{-1}q^{n})}, with q=e2​π​i​τq=e^{2\pi i\tau}, ζ=e2​π​i​z\zeta=e^{2\pi iz}. This is the Jacobi triple product identity.

(9)

ϑ′​(0,τ+1)=eπ​i4​ϑ′​(0,τ)\vartheta^{\prime}(0;\tau+1)=e^{\frac{\pi i}{4}}\vartheta^{\prime}(0;\tau) and ϑ′​(0,−1τ)=(−i​τ)3/2​ϑ′​(0,τ)\vartheta^{\prime}(0;-\frac{1}{\tau})=(-i\tau)^{3/2}\ \vartheta^{\prime}(0;\tau).

(10)

ϑ′​(0,τ)=−2​π​η​(τ)3\vartheta^{\prime}(0;\tau)=-2\pi\eta(\tau)^{3}, with η\eta as in the introduction.

We now turn to the normalized version of Lerch’s function:

Proposition 1.4

For u,v∈𝐂∖(𝐙​τ+𝐙)u,v\in\mathbf{C}\setminus(\mathbf{Z}\tau+\mathbf{Z}) and τ∈ℋ\tau\in\mathcal{H}, define

u↦μ⁡(u,v)u\mapsto\mu(u,v) is a meromorphic function, with simple poles in the points u=n​τ+mu=n\tau+m (n,m∈𝐙)(n,m\in\mathbf{Z}), and residue −12​π​i​1ϑ⁡(v)\frac{-1}{2\pi i}\frac{1}{\vartheta(v)} in u=0u=0,

(1) is trivial and (2) follows from (1) of Proposition 1.3.
(3) The definition of ϑ\vartheta gives the following:

ie−πiτ/4+πivϑ(v)=∑n∈𝐙(−1)neπ​i​(n2−n)​τ+2​π​i​n​v=∑n∈𝐙(−1)n​eπ​i​(n2−n)​τ+2​π​i​n​v1−e2​π​i​n​τ+2​π​i​u​(1−e2​π​i​n​τ+2​π​i​u)=−e2​π​i​v∑n∈𝐙(−1)n​eπ​i​(n2+n)​τ+2​π​i​n​v1−e2​π​i​n​τ+2​π​i​(u+τ)−e2​π​i​u∑n∈𝐙(−1)n​eπ​i​(n2+n)​τ+2​π​i​n​v1−e2​π​i​n​τ+2​π​i​u.\begin{split}i&e^{-\pi i\tau/4+\pi iv}\vartheta(v)=\sum_{n\in\mathbf{Z}}(-1)^{n}e^{\pi i(n^{2}-n)\tau+2\pi inv}\\ &=\sum_{n\in\mathbf{Z}}\frac{(-1)^{n}e^{\pi i(n^{2}-n)\tau+2\pi inv}}{1-e^{2\pi in\tau+2\pi iu}}\left(1-e^{2\pi in\tau+2\pi iu}\right)\\ &=-e^{2\pi iv}\sum_{n\in\mathbf{Z}}\frac{(-1)^{n}e^{\pi i(n^{2}+n)\tau+2\pi inv}}{1-e^{2\pi in\tau+2\pi i(u+\tau)}}-e^{2\pi iu}\sum_{n\in\mathbf{Z}}\frac{(-1)^{n}e^{\pi i(n^{2}+n)\tau+2\pi inv}}{1-e^{2\pi in\tau+2\pi iu}}.\end{split}

Dividing both sides by −eπ​i​u​ϑ​(v)-e^{\pi iu}\vartheta(v), we get the desired result.

μ(u,v)=−e−π​i​uϑ⁡(v)∑n∈𝐙(−1)n​eπ​i​(n2+n)​τ−2​π​i​n​v1−e2​π​i​n​τ−2​π​i​u.\mu(u,v)=-\frac{e^{-\pi iu}}{\vartheta(v)}\sum_{n\in\mathbf{Z}}\frac{(-1)^{n}e^{\pi i(n^{2}+n)\tau-2\pi inv}}{1-e^{2\pi in\tau-2\pi iu}}.

Now using (4) of Proposition 1.3 we find

The pole in u=0u=0 comes from the term n=0n=0. We see

{f⁡(z+1)=f⁡(z)f⁡(z+τ)=e−2​π​i​τ−2​π​i​(u+v+2​z)​f​(z).\begin{cases}f(z+1)=f(z)&\\ f(z+\tau)=e^{-2\pi i\tau-2\pi i(u+v+2z)}f(z).&\end{cases}

It follows that the quotient f⁡(z)/ϑ⁡(z)​ϑ​(u+v+z)f(z)/\vartheta(z)\vartheta(u+v+z) is a double periodic function with at most one simple pole in each fundamental parallelogram, and hence constant:

Proposition 1.5

Let μ\mu be as in Proposition 1.4. Then μ\mu satisfies the following modular transformation properties:

(1)

μ⁡(u,v,τ+1)=e−π​i4​μ​(u,v,τ),\displaystyle{\mu(u,v;\tau+1)=e^{-\frac{\pi i}{4}}\mu(u,v;\tau),}

(2)

1−i​τ​eπ​i​(u−v)2/τ​μ​(uτ,vτ,−1τ)+μ⁡(u,v,τ)=12​i​h​(u−v,τ)\displaystyle{\frac{1}{\sqrt{-i\tau}}\ e^{\pi i(u-v)^{2}/\tau}\mu\left(\frac{u}{\tau},\frac{v}{\tau};-\frac{1}{\tau}\right)+\mu(u,v;\tau)=\frac{1}{2i}h(u-v;\tau)},
with hh as in Definition 1.1.

Proof.

(1) Use (6) of Proposition 1.3.
(2) Replacing (u,v,z,τ)(u,v,z,\tau) by (uτ,vτ,zτ,−1τ)(\frac{u}{\tau},\frac{v}{\tau},\frac{z}{\tau},-\frac{1}{\tau}) in (7) of Proposition 1.4 and using (7) and (9) of Proposition 1.3 we see that the left hand side depends only on u−vu-v, not on uu and vv separately. Call it 12​i​h~​(u−v,τ)\frac{1}{2i}\tilde{h}(u-v;\tau). Using (1) and (3) of Proposition 1.4 we see that h~\tilde{h} satisfies the two identities (1) and (2) of Proposition 1.2, so if we can prove that h~\tilde{h} is a holomorphic function, then we may conclude that h~=h\tilde{h}=h, as desired.

The poles of both u↦μ⁡(u,v)u\mapsto\mu(u,v) and u↦μ⁡(uτ,vτ,−1τ)u\mapsto\mu(\frac{u}{\tau},\frac{v}{\tau};-\frac{1}{\tau}) are simple, and occur at u∈𝐙​τ+𝐙u\in\mathbf{Z}\tau+\mathbf{Z}, so the only poles of u↦h~​(u−v)u\mapsto\tilde{h}(u-v) could be simple poles for u∈𝐙​τ+𝐙u\in\mathbf{Z}\tau+\mathbf{Z}. Since this is a function of u−vu-v it has no poles at all, and hence is holomorphic.

Alternatively, we can check, using (6) of Proposition 1.4 and (7) of Proposition 1.3, that the residue at u=0u=0 vanishes. By (1) and (3) of Proposition 1.4 the residues vanish for all u∈𝐙​τ+𝐙u\in\mathbf{Z}\tau+\mathbf{Z}, hence h~\tilde{h} is holomorphic. ∎

4 A real-analytic Jacobi form?

Definition 1.6

For z∈𝐂z\in\mathbf{C} we define

E⁡(z)=2​∫0ze−π​u2​𝑑u=∑n=0∞(−π)nn!​z2​n+1n+1/2.E(z)=2\int_{0}^{z}e^{-\pi u^{2}}du=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-\pi)^{n}}{n!}\frac{z^{2n+1}}{n+1/2}.

This is an odd entire function of zz.

Lemma 1.7

For z∈𝐑z\in\mathbf{R} we have

E⁡(z)=sgn⁡(z)​(1−β⁡(z2)),E(z)=\operatorname{sgn}(z)\left(1-\beta(z^{2})\right),

where

β⁡(x)=∫x∞u−12​e−π​u​𝑑u(x∈𝐑≥0).\beta(x)=\int_{x}^{\infty}u^{-\frac{1}{2}}e^{-\pi u}du\qquad(x\in\mathbf{R}_{\geq 0}).
Proof.

Write ∫0ze−π​u2​𝑑u\int_{0}^{z}e^{-\pi u^{2}}du as sgn⁡(z)​∫0|z|e−π​u2​𝑑u\operatorname{sgn}(z)\int_{0}^{|z|}e^{-\pi u^{2}}du and substitute u=vu=\sqrt{v}. ∎

We consider for u∈𝐂u\in\mathbf{C} and τ∈ℋ\tau\in\mathcal{H} the series

R⁡(u,τ)=∑ν∈12+𝐙{sgn⁡(ν)−E⁡((ν+a)​2​y)}​(−1)ν−12​e−π​i​ν2​τ−2​π​i​ν​u,R(u;\tau)=\sum_{\nu\in\frac{1}{2}+\mathbf{Z}}\Bigl\{\operatorname{sgn}(\nu)-E\Bigl((\nu+a)\sqrt{2y}\Bigr)\Bigr\}\ (-1)^{\nu-\frac{1}{2}}e^{-\pi i\nu^{2}\tau-2\pi i\nu u},

with y=Im⁡(τ)y=\operatorname{Im}(\tau) and a=Im⁡(u)Im⁡(τ)a=\frac{\operatorname{Im}(u)}{\operatorname{Im}(\tau)}.

Lemma 1.8

For all c,ϵ>0c,\epsilon>0, this series converges absolutely and uniformly on the set {u∈𝐂,τ∈ℋ∣|a|<c,y>ϵ}\{u\in\mathbf{C},\tau\in\mathcal{H}\mid|a|<c,y>\epsilon\}. The function RR it defines is real-analytic and satisfies

∂R∂u¯(u;τ)=2y−1/2e−2​π​a2​yϑ(u¯;−τ¯)\frac{\partial R}{\partial\overline{u}}(u;\tau)=\sqrt{2}y^{-1/2}e^{-2\pi a^{2}y}\vartheta(\overline{u};-\overline{\tau}) (7)

and

∂∂τ¯R(aτ−b;τ)=−i2​ye−2​π​a2​y∑ν∈12+𝐙(−1)ν−12(ν+a)e−π​i​ν2​τ¯−2​π​i​ν​(a​τ¯−b).\frac{\partial}{\partial\overline{\tau}}R(a\tau-b;\tau)=-\frac{i}{\sqrt{2y}}e^{-2\pi a^{2}y}\sum_{\nu\in\frac{1}{2}+\mathbf{Z}}(-1)^{\nu-\frac{1}{2}}(\nu+a)e^{-\pi i\nu^{2}\overline{\tau}-2\pi i\nu(a\overline{\tau}-b)}. (8)
Proof.

We split sgn⁡(ν)−E⁡((ν+a)​2​y)\operatorname{sgn}(\nu)-E((\nu+a)\sqrt{2y}) into the sum of sgn⁡(ν)−sgn⁡((ν+a)​2​y)\operatorname{sgn}(\nu)-\operatorname{sgn}((\nu+a)\sqrt{2y}) and sgn⁡((ν+a)​2​y)​β​(2​(ν+a)2​y)\operatorname{sgn}((\nu+a)\sqrt{2y})\beta(2(\nu+a)^{2}y). We see that sgn⁡(ν)−sgn⁡((ν+a)​2​y)\operatorname{sgn}(\nu)-\operatorname{sgn}((\nu+a)\sqrt{2y}) is nonzero for only a finite number of values ν∈12+𝐙\nu\in\frac{1}{2}+\mathbf{Z} (this number depends on aa, but since aa is bounded, so is this number). Hence the series

∑ν∈12+𝐙{sgn⁡(ν)−sgn⁡((ν+a)​2​y)}​(−1)ν−12​e−π​i​ν2​τ−2​π​i​ν​u\sum_{\nu\in\frac{1}{2}+\mathbf{Z}}\Bigl\{\operatorname{sgn}(\nu)-\operatorname{sgn}\Bigl((\nu+a)\sqrt{2y}\Bigr)\Bigr\}(-1)^{\nu-\frac{1}{2}}e^{-\pi i\nu^{2}\tau-2\pi i\nu u}

converges absolutely and uniformly.

We can easily see that 0≤β⁡(x)≤e−π​x0\leq\beta(x)\leq e^{-\pi x} for all x∈𝐑≥0x\in\mathbf{R}_{\geq 0}, hence

|{sgn⁡((ν+a)​2​y)​β​(2​(ν+a)2​y)}​(−1)ν−12​e−π​i​ν2​τ−2​π​i​ν​u|≤e−2​π​(ν+a)2​y​|e−π​i​ν2​τ−2​π​i​ν​u|=e−π​(ν+a)2​y−π​a2​y≤e−π​(ν+a)2​ϵ.\begin{split}&\left|\left\{\operatorname{sgn}\Bigl((\nu+a)\sqrt{2y}\Bigr)\beta\Bigl(2(\nu+a)^{2}y\Bigr)\right\}(-1)^{\nu-\frac{1}{2}}e^{-\pi i\nu^{2}\tau-2\pi i\nu u}\right|\\ &\leq e^{-2\pi(\nu+a)^{2}y}\left|e^{-\pi i\nu^{2}\tau-2\pi i\nu u}\right|\\ &=e^{-\pi(\nu+a)^{2}y-\pi a^{2}y}\leq e^{-\pi(\nu+a)^{2}\epsilon}.\end{split}

We have the inequality

(ν+a)2≥12​ν2,(\nu+a)^{2}\geq\frac{1}{2}\nu^{2},

for |ν|≥ν0|\nu|\geq\nu_{0}, for some ν0∈𝐑\nu_{0}\in\mathbf{R} which depends only on cc (aa is bounded by cc). Hence we see that the series

∑ν∈12+𝐙{sgn⁡((ν+a)​2​y)​β​(2​(ν+a)2​y)}​(−1)ν−12​e−π​i​ν2​τ−2​π​i​ν​u\sum_{\nu\in\frac{1}{2}+\mathbf{Z}}\left\{\operatorname{sgn}\Bigl((\nu+a)\sqrt{2y}\Bigr)\beta\Bigl(2(\nu+a)^{2}y\Bigr)\right\}(-1)^{\nu-\frac{1}{2}}e^{-\pi i\nu^{2}\tau-2\pi i\nu u}

converges absolutely and uniformly on the given set.

Since RR is the (infinite) sum of real-analytic functions, and the series converges absolutely and uniformly, it is real-analytic.

We fix τ∈ℋ\tau\in\mathcal{H}, and determine u=a​τ−bu=a\tau-b by the coordinates a,b∈𝐑a,b\in\mathbf{R}. We see

(∂∂a+τ​∂∂b)​R​(a​τ−b,τ)\displaystyle\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial a}+\tau\frac{\partial}{\partial b}\right)R(a\tau-b;\tau)
=(∂∂a+τ​∂∂b)​∑ν∈12+𝐙{sgn⁡(ν)−E⁡((ν+a)​2​y)}​(−1)ν−12​e−π​i​ν2​τ−2​π​i​ν​(a​τ−b)\displaystyle=\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial a}+\tau\frac{\partial}{\partial b}\right)\sum_{\nu\in\frac{1}{2}+\mathbf{Z}}\left\{\operatorname{sgn}(\nu)-E\Bigl((\nu+a)\sqrt{2y}\Bigr)\right\}(-1)^{\nu-\frac{1}{2}}e^{-\pi i\nu^{2}\tau-2\pi i\nu(a\tau-b)}
=−2​y∑ν∈12+𝐙E′((ν+a)2​y)(−1)ν−12e−π​i​ν2​τ−2​π​i​ν​(a​τ−b)\displaystyle=-\sqrt{2y}\sum_{\nu\in\frac{1}{2}+\mathbf{Z}}E^{\prime}\Bigl((\nu+a)\sqrt{2y}\Bigr)(-1)^{\nu-\frac{1}{2}}e^{-\pi i\nu^{2}\tau-2\pi i\nu(a\tau-b)}
=−22​y∑ν∈12+𝐙e−2​π​(ν+a)2​y(−1)ν−12e−π​i​ν2​τ−2​π​i​ν​(a​τ−b)\displaystyle=-2\sqrt{2y}\sum_{\nu\in\frac{1}{2}+\mathbf{Z}}e^{-2\pi(\nu+a)^{2}y}(-1)^{\nu-\frac{1}{2}}e^{-\pi i\nu^{2}\tau-2\pi i\nu(a\tau-b)}
=−22​ye−2​π​a2​y∑ν∈12+𝐙(−1)ν−12e−π​i​ν2​τ¯−2​π​i​ν​(a​τ¯−b)\displaystyle=-2\sqrt{2y}e^{-2\pi a^{2}y}\sum_{\nu\in\frac{1}{2}+\mathbf{Z}}(-1)^{\nu-\frac{1}{2}}e^{-\pi i\nu^{2}\overline{\tau}-2\pi i\nu(a\overline{\tau}-b)}
=−2​i​2​y​e−2​π​a2​y​ϑ​(a​τ¯−b,−τ¯),\displaystyle=-2i\sqrt{2y}e^{-2\pi a^{2}y}\vartheta(a\overline{\tau}-b;-\overline{\tau}),

with ϑ\vartheta as in Proposition 1.3 and the term-by-term differentiation being easily justified. Since ∂∂u¯=i2​y​(∂∂a+τ​∂∂b)\frac{\partial}{\partial\overline{u}}=\frac{i}{2y}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial a}+\tau\frac{\partial}{\partial b}\right), this gives the differential equation (7). Similarly

∂∂τ¯​R​(a​τ−b,τ)=12​(∂∂x+i​∂∂y)​∑ν∈12+𝐙{sgn⁡(ν)−E⁡((ν+a)​2​y)}​(−1)ν−12​e−π​i​ν2​τ−2​π​i​ν​(a​τ−b)=−i212​y∑ν∈12+𝐙(ν+a)E′((ν+a)2​y)(−1)ν−12e−π​i​ν2​τ−2​π​i​ν​(a​τ−b)=−i2​ye−2​π​a2​y∑ν∈12+𝐙(−1)ν−12(ν+a)e−π​i​ν2​τ¯−2​π​i​ν​(a​τ¯−b),\begin{split}&\frac{\partial}{\partial\overline{\tau}}R(a\tau-b;\tau)\\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x}+i\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\right)\sum_{\nu\in\frac{1}{2}+\mathbf{Z}}\left\{\operatorname{sgn}(\nu)-E\Bigl((\nu+a)\sqrt{2y}\Bigr)\right\}(-1)^{\nu-\frac{1}{2}}e^{-\pi i\nu^{2}\tau-2\pi i\nu(a\tau-b)}\\ &=-\frac{i}{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2y}}\sum_{\nu\in\frac{1}{2}+\mathbf{Z}}(\nu+a)\ E^{\prime}\Bigl((\nu+a)\sqrt{2y}\Bigr)\ (-1)^{\nu-\frac{1}{2}}e^{-\pi i\nu^{2}\tau-2\pi i\nu(a\tau-b)}\\ &=-\frac{i}{\sqrt{2y}}e^{-2\pi a^{2}y}\sum_{\nu\in\frac{1}{2}+\mathbf{Z}}(-1)^{\nu-\frac{1}{2}}(\nu+a)\ e^{-\pi i\nu^{2}\overline{\tau}-2\pi i\nu(a\overline{\tau}-b)},\end{split}

proving equation (8). ∎

Proposition 1.9

The function RR has the following elliptic transformation properties:

(1)

R⁡(u+1)=−R⁡(u)R(u+1)=-R(u),

(2)

R⁡(u)+e−2​π​i​u−π​i​τ​R​(u+τ)=2​e−π​i​u−π​i​τ/4R(u)+e^{-2\pi iu-\pi i\tau}R(u+\tau)=2e^{-\pi iu-\pi i\tau/4},

(3)

R⁡(−u)=R⁡(u)R(-u)=R(u).

Proof.

Part (1) is trivial, and for (3) we replace ν\nu by −ν-\nu in the sum and use the fact that EE is an odd function. To prove (2), we start with

Remark 1.12

Parts (1) and (2) of the theorem say that the function μ~\tilde{\mu} transforms like a two-variable Jacobi form of weight 12\frac{1}{2} and index (−111−1)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-1&1\\ 1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right) (for the theory of Jacobi forms, see [9], where, however, only Jacobi forms of one variable are considered). Furthermore we can find several differential equations satisfied by μ~\tilde{\mu}. Therefore we would like to call this function a real-analytic Jacobi form. However, in the literature I haven’t been able to find a satisfying definition of a real-analytic Jacobi form. I intend to return to this problem in the future.

5 Period integrals of weight 3/2 unary theta functions

In this section we will rewrite hh in terms of the period integral of a unary theta function of weight 3/2.

To state the main result we need the following definition:

Definition 1.14

Let a,b∈𝐑a,b\in\mathbf{R} and τ∈ℋ\tau\in\mathcal{H} then

ga,b​(τ):=∑ν∈a+𝐙ν​eπ​i​ν2​τ+2​π​i​ν​b.g_{a,b}(\tau):=\sum_{\nu\in a+\mathbf{Z}}\nu e^{\pi i\nu^{2}\tau+2\pi i\nu b}.

The function ga,bg_{a,b} is a unary theta function.

Proposition 1.15

ga,bg_{a,b} satisfies:

(1)

ga+1,b​(τ)=ga,b​(τ)g_{a+1,b}(\tau)=g_{a,b}(\tau)

(2)

ga,b+1​(τ)=e2​π​i​a​ga,b​(τ)g_{a,b+1}(\tau)=e^{2\pi ia}g_{a,b}(\tau)

(3)

g−a,−b​(τ)=−ga,b​(τ)g_{-a,-b}(\tau)=-g_{a,b}(\tau)

(4)

ga,b​(τ+1)=e−π​i​a​(a+1)​ga,a+b+12​(τ)g_{a,b}(\tau+1)=e^{-\pi ia(a+1)}g_{a,a+b+\frac{1}{2}}(\tau)

(5)

ga,b​(−1τ)=i​e2​π​i​a​b​(−i​τ)32​gb,−a​(τ)g_{a,b}(-\frac{1}{\tau})=ie^{2\pi iab}(-i\tau)^{\frac{3}{2}}g_{b,-a}(\tau)

I will not prove these relations, since they are all easy. For (5) use Poisson summation.
From these relations it follows that if aa and bb are rational, the function ga,bg_{a,b} is a modular form of weight 3/2.

Theorem 1.16

Let τ∈ℋ\tau\in\mathcal{H}, then

(1)

for a∈(−12,12)a\in(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}) and b∈𝐑b\in\mathbf{R}

∫−τ¯i​∞ga+12,b+12​(z)−i⁡(z+τ)​𝑑z=−e−π​i​a2​τ+2​π​i​a​(b+12)​R​(a​τ−b),\int_{-\overline{\tau}}^{i\infty}\frac{g_{a+\frac{1}{2},b+\frac{1}{2}}(z)}{\sqrt{-i(z+\tau)}}\,dz=-e^{-\pi ia^{2}\tau+2\pi ia(b+\frac{1}{2})}R(a\tau-b),

with RR as in Lemma 1.8.

(2)

for a,b∈(−12,12)a,b\in(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})

∫0i​∞ga+12,b+12​(z)−i⁡(z+τ)​𝑑z=−e−π​i​a2​τ+2​π​i​a​(b+12)​h​(a​τ−b),\int_{0}^{i\infty}\frac{g_{a+\frac{1}{2},b+\frac{1}{2}}(z)}{\sqrt{-i(z+\tau)}}\,dz=-e^{-\pi ia^{2}\tau+2\pi ia(b+\frac{1}{2})}h(a\tau-b),

with hh as in Definition 1.1.

Remark 1.17

The left hand side in (2) is 1-periodic as a function of aa and, up to a factor, as a function of bb, while the right hand side is not.

For the proof we need the following two lemmas:

Lemma 1.18

If r∈𝐑r\in\mathbf{R}, r≠0r\not=0, and τ∈ℋ\tau\in\mathcal{H} then

∫−∞∞eπ​i​τ​w2w+i​rdw=−πr∫0i​∞eπ​i​r2​z−i⁡(z+τ)dz.\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{\pi i\tau w^{2}}}{w+ir}\,dw=-\pi r\int_{0}^{i\infty}\frac{e^{\pi ir^{2}z}}{\sqrt{-i(z+\tau)}}\,dz.
Proof.

Both sides define a holomorphic function of τ∈ℋ\tau\in\mathcal{H}. So we only have to prove the identity for τ=i​t\tau=it, with t∈𝐑>0t\in\mathbf{R}_{>0}. The identity then becomes

∫−∞∞e−π​t​w2w+i​rdw=−πir∫0∞e−π​r2​uu+tdu,\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{-\pi tw^{2}}}{w+ir}\,dw=-\pi ir\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{e^{-\pi r^{2}u}}{\sqrt{u+t}}\,du,

where we have substituted z=i​uz=iu in the integral on the right. We can easily see that both sides, considered as functions of tt, are solutions of (−∂∂t+π​r2)​f​(t)=−π​i​rt(-\frac{\partial}{\partial t}+\pi r^{2})f(t)=-\frac{\pi ir}{\sqrt{t}}:

(−∂∂t+π​r2)​LHS=π∫−∞∞(w−ir)e−π​t​w2dw=−πir∫−∞∞e−π​t​w2dw=−π​i​rt,(−∂∂t+π​r2)​RHS=−eπ​r2​t​∂∂t​(e−π​r2​t​RHS)=π​i​r​eπ​r2​t​∂∂t​∫t∞e−π​r2​xx​dx=−π​i​rt.\begin{split}\Bigl(-\frac{\partial}{\partial t}+\pi r^{2}\Bigr)\operatorname{LHS}&=\pi\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(w-ir)e^{-\pi tw^{2}}dw=-\pi ir\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-\pi tw^{2}}dw=-\frac{\pi ir}{\sqrt{t}},\\ \left(-\frac{\partial}{\partial t}+\pi r^{2}\right)\operatorname{RHS}&=-e^{\pi r^{2}t}\frac{\partial}{\partial t}(e^{-\pi r^{2}t}\operatorname{RHS})=\pi ire^{\pi r^{2}t}\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_{t}^{\infty}\frac{e^{-\pi r^{2}x}}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx=-\frac{\pi ir}{\sqrt{t}}.\end{split}

Both sides have the same limit 0 as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty, hence they are equal. ∎

Lemma 1.19

Let b∈(−12,12)b\in(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}) and let z∈𝐂z\in\mathbf{C}, such that z∉(12+𝐙)​iz\not\in\left(\frac{1}{2}+\mathbf{Z}\right)i, then

−e2​π​b​zcosh⁡π​z=1π​∑ν∈12+𝐙e2​π​i​ν​(b+12)z−i​ν.-\frac{e^{2\pi bz}}{\cosh\pi z}=\frac{1}{\pi}\sum_{\nu\in\frac{1}{2}+\mathbf{Z}}\frac{e^{2\pi i\nu(b+\frac{1}{2})}}{z-i\nu}.
Proof.

We first show that the series on the right hand side converges (it doesn’t converge absolutely). Since Dirichlet’s test for convergence (see [28, pp. 17]) is not directly applicable, we prove this by means of partial summation (we could also do this by comparing the series with the series ∑n∈𝐙≠0e2​π​i​n​(b+12)n)\sum_{n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\not=0}}\frac{e^{2\pi in(b+\frac{1}{2})}}{n}): Define

Tν:=e2​π​i​(ν+1)​(b+12)e2​π​i​(b+12)−1,T_{\nu}:=\frac{e^{2\pi i(\nu+1)(b+\frac{1}{2})}}{e^{2\pi i(b+\frac{1}{2})}-1},

then Tν−Tν−1=e2​π​i​ν​(b+12)T_{\nu}-T_{\nu-1}=e^{2\pi i\nu(b+\frac{1}{2})} and |Tν|=1|e2​π​i​(b+12)−1||T_{\nu}|=\frac{1}{|e^{2\pi i(b+\frac{1}{2})}-1|}. Hence

∑ν∈12+𝐙ν0≤ν≤ν1​e2​π​i​ν​(b+12)z−i​ν=∑ν∈12+𝐙ν0≤ν≤ν1​Tν−Tν−1z−i​ν=−i​∑ν∈12+𝐙ν0≤ν≤ν1​Tν(z−i​ν)​(z−i⁡(ν+1))−Tν0−1z−i​ν0+Tν1z−i⁡(ν1+1),\begin{split}&\underset{\nu_{0}\leq\nu\leq\nu_{1}}{\sum_{\nu\in\frac{1}{2}+\mathbf{Z}}}\frac{e^{2\pi i\nu(b+\frac{1}{2})}}{z-i\nu}=\underset{\nu_{0}\leq\nu\leq\nu_{1}}{\sum_{\nu\in\frac{1}{2}+\mathbf{Z}}}\frac{T_{\nu}-T_{\nu-1}}{z-i\nu}\\ &=-i\underset{\nu_{0}\leq\nu\leq\nu_{1}}{\sum_{\nu\in\frac{1}{2}+\mathbf{Z}}}\frac{T_{\nu}}{(z-i\nu)(z-i(\nu+1))}-\frac{T_{\nu_{0}-1}}{z-i\nu_{0}}+\frac{T_{\nu_{1}}}{z-i(\nu_{1}+1)},\end{split}

of Theorem 1.16.

(1) We see

Chapter 2 Indefinite ϑ\vartheta-functions

6 Introduction

The classical theta series associated to a positive definite quadratic form Q:𝐑r⟶𝐑Q:\mathbf{R}^{r}\longrightarrow\mathbf{R} and B:𝐑r×𝐑r⟶𝐑B:\mathbf{R}^{r}\times\mathbf{R}^{r}\longrightarrow\mathbf{R}, the associated bilinear form B⁡(x,y)=Q⁡(x+y)−Q⁡(x)−Q⁡(y)B(x,y)=Q(x+y)-Q(x)-Q(y), is the series

Θ⁡(z,τ):=∑n∈𝐙re2​π​i​Q​(n)​τ+2​π​i​B​(n,z).\Theta(z;\tau):=\sum_{n\in\mathbf{Z}^{r}}e^{2\pi iQ(n)\tau+2\pi iB(n,z)}. (19)

These theta series have well-known transformation properties. In particular Θ⁡(0,τ)\Theta(0;\tau) is a modular form of weight r/2r/2.

In [11] Göttsche and Zagier define a theta function for the case when the type of QQ is (r−1,1)(r-1,1). The definition of these functions is almost the same as in (19), only here the sum doesn’t run over 𝐙r\mathbf{Z}^{r}, but some appropriate subset. However, in general, these functions do not have nice modular transformation properties.

In this chapter we give a modified definition. We find elliptic and modular transformation properties for these functions. The theta functions we define depend not only on QQ, but also on two vectors c1,c2∈𝐑rc_{1},c_{2}\in\mathbf{R}^{r} with Q⁡(ci)≤0Q(c_{i})\leq 0, i=1,2i=1,2. The case Q⁡(c1)=Q⁡(c2)=0Q(c_{1})=Q(c_{2})=0 gives the same functions as in [11].

There is a connection between the indefinite ϑ\vartheta-functions from this chapter and certain ϑ\vartheta-functions considered by Siegel (see [25]). However, I will not give this connection here.

7 Definition of ϑ\vartheta

Let AA be a symmetric r×rr\times r-matrix with integer coefficients, which is non-degenerate. We consider the quadratic form Q:𝐂r⟶𝐂Q:\mathbf{C}^{r}\longrightarrow\mathbf{C}, Q⁡(x)=12​⟨x,A​x⟩Q(x)=\frac{1}{2}\left<x,Ax\right> and the associated bilinear form B⁡(x,y)=⟨x,A​y⟩=Q⁡(x+y)−Q⁡(x)−Q⁡(y)B(x,y)=\left<x,Ay\right>=Q(x+y)-Q(x)-Q(y).

The type of QQ is the pair (r−s,s)(r-s,s), where ss is the largest dimension of a linear subspace of 𝐑r\mathbf{R}^{r} on which QQ is negative definite. The signature of QQ is the number r−2​sr-2s.

From now on we assume that s=1s=1, i.e., that QQ has type (r−1,1)(r-1,1). Then the set of vectors c∈𝐑rc\in\mathbf{R}^{r} with Q⁡(c)<0Q(c)<0 has two components. If B⁡(c1,c2)<0B(c_{1},c_{2})<0 then c1c_{1} and c2c_{2} belong to the same component, while if B⁡(c1,c2)>0B(c_{1},c_{2})>0 then c1c_{1} and c2c_{2} belong to opposite components. Let CQC_{Q} be one of the two components. If c0c_{0} is a vector in that component, then CQC_{Q} is given by:

CQ:={c∈𝐑r∣Q(c)<0,B(c,c0)<0}.C_{Q}:=\{c\in\mathbf{R}^{r}\mid Q(c)<0,\ B(c,c_{0})<0\}.

We further set

SQ:={c∈𝐙r∣cprimitive,Q(c)=0,B(c,c0)<0}.S_{Q}:=\{c\in\mathbf{Z}^{r}\mid c\text{ primitive},\ Q(c)=0,\ B(c,c_{0})<0\}.

(cc primitive means that the greatest common divisor of the components of cc is 1). The (r−1)(r-1)-dimensional hyperbolic space CQ/𝐑+C_{Q}/\mathbf{R}_{+} is the natural domain of definition of automorphic forms with respect to OA+​(𝐙)O_{A}^{+}(\mathbf{Z}) (see section 2.4 for the definition), and SQS_{Q} is a set of representatives for the corresponding set of cusps

{c∈𝐐r∣Q(c)=0,B(c,c0)<0}/𝐐+.\{c\in\mathbf{Q}^{r}\mid Q(c)=0,\ B(c,c_{0})<0\}/\mathbf{Q}_{+}.

Note that SQS_{Q} is empty in some cases, for example if A=(100−3)A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\ 0&-3\end{smallmatrix}\right). Further we put C¯Q:=CQ∪SQ\overline{C}_{Q}:=C_{Q}\cup S_{Q}. This is a generalisation of the usual construction ℋ¯=ℋ∪ℙ1​(𝐐)\overline{\mathcal{H}}=\mathcal{H}\cup\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbf{Q}), which is the special cone C¯Q=CQ∪SQ\overline{C}_{Q}=C_{Q}\cup S_{Q} for the quadratic form Q⁡(a,b,c)=12​(b2−4​a​c)Q(a,b,c)=\frac{1}{2}(b^{2}-4ac).

For c∈C¯Qc\in\overline{C}_{Q} put

R⁡(c)\displaystyle R(c) :={𝐑rif ​c∈CQ{a∈𝐑r∣B⁡(c,a)∉𝐙}if ​c∈SQ\displaystyle:=\begin{cases}\mathbf{R}^{r}&\text{if }c\in C_{Q}\\ \{a\in\mathbf{R}^{r}\mid B(c,a)\not\in\mathbf{Z}\}&\text{if }c\in S_{Q}\end{cases}
and
D⁡(c)\displaystyle D(c) :={(z,τ)∈𝐂r×ℋ∣Im⁡(z)/Im⁡(τ)∈R⁡(c)}.\displaystyle:=\{(z,\tau)\in\mathbf{C}^{r}\times\mathcal{H}\mid\operatorname{Im}(z)/\operatorname{Im}(\tau)\in R(c)\}.
Definition 2.1

Let c1,c2∈C¯Qc_{1},c_{2}\in\overline{C}_{Q}. We define the theta function of QQ with characteristics a∈R⁡(c1)∩R⁡(c2)a\in R(c_{1})\cap R(c_{2}) and b∈𝐑rb\in\mathbf{R}^{r}, with respect to (c1,c2)(c_{1},c_{2}) by

ϑa,b​(τ)=ϑa,bc1,c2​(τ):=∑ν∈a+𝐙rρ⁡(ν,τ)​e2​π​i​Q​(ν)​τ+2​π​i​B​(ν,b),\vartheta_{a,b}(\tau)=\vartheta_{a,b}^{c_{1},c_{2}}(\tau):=\sum_{\nu\in a+\mathbf{Z}^{r}}\rho(\nu;\tau)e^{2\pi iQ(\nu)\tau+2\pi iB(\nu,b)},

ρ⁡(ν,τ)=ρAc1,c2​(ν,τ):=ρc1​(ν,τ)−ρc2​(ν,τ),\rho(\nu;\tau)=\rho^{c_{1},c_{2}}_{A}(\nu;\tau):=\rho^{c_{1}}(\nu;\tau)-\rho^{c_{2}}(\nu;\tau),

with y=Im⁡(τ)y=\operatorname{Im}(\tau) and EE as in Definition 1.6.

For (z,τ)∈D⁡(c1)∩D⁡(c2)(z,\tau)\in D(c_{1})\cap D(c_{2}), we define the theta function of QQ with respect to (c1,c2)(c_{1},c_{2}) by

ϑ⁡(z,τ)=ϑAc1,c2​(z,τ):=e−2​π​i​Q​(a)​τ−2​π​i​B​(a,b)​ϑa,b​(τ)=∑n∈𝐙rρ⁡(n+a,τ)​e2​π​i​Q​(n)​τ+2​π​i​B​(n,z),\begin{split}\vartheta(z;\tau)=\vartheta^{c_{1},c_{2}}_{A}(z;\tau)&:=e^{-2\pi iQ(a)\tau-2\pi iB(a,b)}\vartheta_{a,b}(\tau)\\ &=\sum_{n\in\mathbf{Z}^{r}}\rho(n+a;\tau)e^{2\pi iQ(n)\tau+2\pi iB(n,z)},\end{split}

with a,b∈𝐑ra,b\in\mathbf{R}^{r} defined by z=a​τ+bz=a\tau+b, so a=Im⁡(z)Im⁡(τ)a=\frac{\operatorname{Im}(z)}{\operatorname{Im}(\tau)}, b=Im⁡(z¯​τ)Im⁡(τ)b=\frac{\operatorname{Im}(\overline{z}\tau)}{\operatorname{Im}(\tau)}.

Remark 2.2

The definition doesn’t change if we replace cic_{i} by λ​ci\lambda c_{i}, with λ∈𝐑+\lambda\in\mathbf{R}_{+}. Hence we could replace the condition Q⁡(ci)<0Q(c_{i})<0 by Q⁡(ci)=−1Q(c_{i})=-1. This would simplify the definition of ρ\rho.

Remark 2.3

In some special cases ϑa,b\vartheta_{a,b} is holomorphic: if c1,c2∈SQc_{1},c_{2}\in S_{Q} and, as we will see in section 2.5, also for some special values of c1c_{1}, c2c_{2}, aa and bb. In general however, the functions ϑ\vartheta and ϑa,b\vartheta_{a,b} are not holomorphic.

Because QQ is indefinite, e2​π​i​Q​(n)​τe^{2\pi iQ(n)\tau} isn’t bounded. Therefore it’s not immediately clear that the series defining ϑ⁡(z,τ)\vartheta(z;\tau) converges absolutely. However, using an estimate for the growth of ρ\rho we shall find:

Proposition 2.4

The series defining ϑ⁡(z,τ)\vartheta(z;\tau) converges absolutely.

For the proof of this proposition, we need two lemmas

Lemma 2.6

Let c1,c2∈CQc_{1},c_{2}\in C_{Q} be linearly independent. The quadratic form Q+:𝐑r⟶𝐑Q^{+}:\mathbf{R}^{r}\longrightarrow\mathbf{R}, Q+​(ν):=Q⁡(ν)+B⁡(c1,c2)4​Q​(c1)​Q​(c2)−B​(c1,c2)2​B​(c1,ν)​B​(c2,ν)Q^{+}(\nu):=Q(\nu)+\frac{B(c_{1},c_{2})}{4Q(c_{1})Q(c_{2})-B(c_{1},c_{2})^{2}}B(c_{1},\nu)B(c_{2},\nu) is positive definite.

8 Properties of the ϑ\vartheta-functions

The theta functions in Definition 2.1 have some nice elliptic and modular transformation properties, similar to those of the theta functions associated to positive definite quadratic forms.

Proposition 2.7

The function ϑ\vartheta satisfies:

  • (1)

    For c1,c2,c3∈C¯Qc_{1},c_{2},c_{3}\in\overline{C}_{Q} and (z,τ)∈D⁡(c1)∩D⁡(c2)∩D⁡(c3)(z,\tau)\in D(c_{1})\cap D(c_{2})\cap D(c_{3}) we have the cocycle conditions ϑc1,c2+ϑc2,c1=0\vartheta^{c_{1},c_{2}}+\vartheta^{c_{2},c_{1}}=0 and ϑc1,c2+ϑc2,c3+ϑc3,c1=0\vartheta^{c_{1},c_{2}}+\vartheta^{c_{2},c_{3}}+\vartheta^{c_{3},c_{1}}=0.

  • (2)

    ϑ⁡(z+λ​τ+μ,τ)=e−2​π​i​Q​(λ)​τ−2​π​i​B​(z,λ)​ϑ​(z,τ)\vartheta(z+\lambda\tau+\mu;\tau)=e^{-2\pi iQ(\lambda)\tau-2\pi iB(z,\lambda)}\vartheta(z;\tau) for all λ∈𝐙r\lambda\in\mathbf{Z}^{r} and μ∈A−1​𝐙r\mu\in A^{-1}\mathbf{Z}^{r}.

  • (3)

    ϑ⁡(−z,τ)=−ϑ⁡(z,τ)\vartheta(-z;\tau)=-\vartheta(z;\tau).

  • (4)

    The function (c1,c2)↦ϑc1,c2(c_{1},c_{2})\mapsto\vartheta^{c_{1},c_{2}} is continuous on CQ×CQC_{Q}\times C_{Q}.

  • (5)

    Let c1,c3∈CQc_{1},c_{3}\in C_{Q}, c2∈SQc_{2}\in S_{Q} and (z,τ)∈D⁡(c2)(z,\tau)\in D(c_{2}). Set c⁡(t)=c2+t​c3c(t)=c_{2}+tc_{3}. Then c⁡(t)∈CQc(t)\in C_{Q} for all t∈(0,∞)t\in(0,\infty) and limt↓0ϑc1,c⁡(t)​(z,τ)=ϑc1,c2​(z,τ)\lim_{t\downarrow 0}\vartheta^{c_{1},c(t)}(z;\tau)=\vartheta^{c_{1},c_{2}}(z;\tau).

  • (6)

    ϑ⁡(z,τ+1)=ϑ⁡(z+12​A−1​A∗,τ)\vartheta(z;\tau+1)=\vartheta(z+\frac{1}{2}A^{-1}A^{*};\tau) with A∗=(A11​…​Ar​r)T∈𝐙rA^{*}=(A_{11}\ldots A_{rr})^{T}\in\mathbf{Z}^{r}, the vector of diagonal elements of AA. In particular, ϑ⁡(z,τ+2)=ϑ⁡(z,τ)\vartheta(z;\tau+2)=\vartheta(z;\tau) and ϑ⁡(z,τ+1)=ϑ⁡(z,τ)\vartheta(z;\tau+1)=\vartheta(z;\tau) if the matrix AA is even.

    Let D′(c):={(z,τ)∈D(c)∣(zτ,−1τ)∈D(c)}={(aτ+b,τ)∣τ∈ℋ,a,b∈𝐑r,B(c,a)∉𝐙,B(c,b)∉𝐙}D^{\prime}(c):=\left\{(z,\tau)\in D(c)\mid\left(\frac{z}{\tau},-\frac{1}{\tau}\right)\in D(c)\right\}=\{(a\tau+b,\tau)\mid\tau\in\mathcal{H},\ a,b\in\mathbf{R}^{r},\ B(c,a)\not\in\mathbf{Z},\ B(c,b)\not\in\mathbf{Z}\}. If (z,τ)∈D′​(c1)∩D′​(c2)(z,\tau)\in D^{\prime}(c_{1})\cap D^{\prime}(c_{2}) then

    ϑ⁡(zτ,−1τ)=i−detA​(−i​τ)r/2​∑p∈A−1​𝐙r/𝐙re2​π​i​Q​(z+p​τ)/τ​ϑ​(z+p​τ,τ).\vartheta\Bigl(\frac{z}{\tau};-\frac{1}{\tau}\Bigr)=\frac{i}{\sqrt{-\det A}}(-i\tau)^{r/2}\sum_{p\in A^{-1}\mathbf{Z}^{r}/\mathbf{Z}^{r}}e^{2\pi iQ(z+p\tau)/\tau}\vartheta(z+p\tau;\tau).
Proof.

(1) follows from the corresponding relations for ρc1,c2\rho^{c_{1},c_{2}}.
(2) The identity ϑ⁡(z+μ,τ)=ϑ⁡(z,τ)\vartheta(z+\mu;\tau)=\vartheta(z;\tau) for μ∈A−1​𝐙r\mu\in A^{-1}\mathbf{Z}^{r} is easy, and we find ϑ⁡(z+λ​τ,τ)=e−2​π​i​Q​(λ)​τ−2​π​i​B​(z,λ)​ϑ​(z,τ)\vartheta(z+\lambda\tau;\tau)=e^{-2\pi iQ(\lambda)\tau-2\pi iB(z,\lambda)}\vartheta(z;\tau) for λ∈𝐙r\lambda\in\mathbf{Z}^{r} when we replace nn by n+λn+\lambda in the definition.

For (3), replace nn by −n-n in the definition and use that EE and sgn\operatorname{sgn} are odd functions.
(4) We show that c1↦ϑc1,c2c_{1}\mapsto\vartheta^{c_{1},c_{2}} is continuous on CQC_{Q}. The result then follows from (1).

Using the decomposition of ρ\rho as the sum of (25), (26) and (27) we see that it’s sufficient to prove that

c↦∑ν∈a+𝐙rsgn⁡(B⁡(c,ν))​β​(−B​(c,ν)2Q⁡(c)​y)​e2​π​i​Q​(ν)​τ+2​π​i​B​(ν,b),c\mapsto\sum_{\nu\in a+\mathbf{Z}^{r}}\operatorname{sgn}\Bigl(B(c,\nu)\Bigr)\beta\left(-\frac{B(c,\nu)^{2}}{Q(c)}y\right)e^{2\pi iQ(\nu)\tau+2\pi iB(\nu,b)}, (33)

and

c1↦∑ν∈a+𝐙r{sgn⁡(B⁡(c1,ν))−sgn⁡(B⁡(c2,ν))}​e2​π​i​Q​(ν)​τ+2​π​i​B​(ν,b)c_{1}\mapsto\sum_{\nu\in a+\mathbf{Z}^{r}}\Bigl\{\operatorname{sgn}\Bigl(B(c_{1},\nu)\Bigr)-\operatorname{sgn}\Bigl(B(c_{2},\nu)\Bigr)\Bigr\}\ e^{2\pi iQ(\nu)\tau+2\pi iB(\nu,b)} (34)

are continuous on CQC_{Q}.

Using Lemma 2.5 and (30) we see

|sgn⁡(B⁡(c,ν))​β​(−B​(c,ν)2Q⁡(c)​y)​e2​π​i​Q​(ν)​τ+2​π​i​B​(ν,b)|≤e−2​π​(Q⁡(ν)−B​(c,ν)22​Q​(c))​y≤e−2​π​λc,c0​Qc0​(ν)​y\begin{split}\left|\operatorname{sgn}\Bigl(B(c,\nu)\Bigr)\beta\left(-\frac{B(c,\nu)^{2}}{Q(c)}y\right)e^{2\pi iQ(\nu)\tau+2\pi iB(\nu,b)}\right|&\leq e^{-2\pi\left(Q(\nu)-\frac{B(c,\nu)^{2}}{2Q(c)}\right)y}\\ &\leq e^{-2\pi\lambda_{c,c_{0}}Q_{c_{0}}(\nu)y}\end{split}

Since c↦λc,c0c\mapsto\lambda_{c,c_{0}} is continuous and λc,c0>0\lambda_{c,c_{0}}>0 for all c∈CQc\in C_{Q}, we can find an neighbourhood 𝒩c\mathcal{N}_{c} of cc such that λc,c0≥ϵ>0\lambda_{c,c_{0}}\geq\epsilon>0 for all c∈𝒩cc\in\mathcal{N}_{c}. Hence on 𝒩c\mathcal{N}_{c} we find

|sgn⁡(B⁡(c,ν))​β​(−B​(c,ν)2Q⁡(c)​y)​e2​π​i​Q​(ν)​τ+2​π​i​B​(ν,b)|≤e−2​π​ϵ​Qc0​(ν)​y.\left|\operatorname{sgn}\Bigl(B(c,\nu)\Bigr)\beta\left(-\frac{B(c,\nu)^{2}}{Q(c)}y\right)e^{2\pi iQ(\nu)\tau+2\pi iB(\nu,b)}\right|\leq e^{-2\pi\epsilon Q_{c_{0}}(\nu)y}.

The series

∑ν∈a+𝐙re−2​π​ϵ​Qc0​(ν)​y\sum_{\nu\in a+\mathbf{Z}^{r}}e^{-2\pi\epsilon Q_{c_{0}}(\nu)y}

converges, and so the series in (33) converges uniformly for cc in 𝒩c\mathcal{N}_{c}. Hence the function in (33) is continuous on 𝒩c\mathcal{N}_{c}. Since this holds for all c∈CQc\in C_{Q}, the function in (33) is continuous on CQC_{Q}.

9 Transformation properties of ϑ\vartheta with respect to OA+​(𝐙)O_{A}^{+}(\mathbf{Z})

We consider the group

OA​(𝐑):={C∈GLr⁡(𝐑)∣Ct​A​C=A}.O_{A}(\mathbf{R}):=\{C\in\operatorname{GL}_{r}(\mathbf{R})\mid C^{t}AC=A\}.

If C∈OA​(𝐑)C\in O_{A}(\mathbf{R}) and c∈CQ⊂𝐑rc\in C_{Q}\subset\mathbf{R}^{r} then Q⁡(C​c)=Q⁡(c)Q(Cc)=Q(c), so C⋅CQC\cdot C_{Q} is either CQC_{Q} or −CQ-C_{Q}. We consider only matrices CC that leave CQC_{Q} invariant, i.e. B⁡(C​c,c)<0B(Cc,c)<0, for all c∈CQc\in C_{Q}. Set

OA+(𝐑):={C∈GLr(𝐑)∣CtAC=A,B(Cc,c)<0∀c∈CQ}.O_{A}^{+}(\mathbf{R}):=\{C\in\operatorname{GL}_{r}(\mathbf{R})\mid C^{t}AC=A,\ B(Cc,c)<0\ \forall c\in C_{Q}\}.

This is a subgroup of OA​(𝐑)O_{A}(\mathbf{R}) of index 2.

Definition 2.10

Let

OA+​(𝐙):=OA+​(𝐑)∩GLr⁡(𝐙).O_{A}^{+}(\mathbf{Z}):=O_{A}^{+}(\mathbf{R})\cap\operatorname{GL}_{r}(\mathbf{Z}).
Remark 2.11

From Ct​A​C=AC^{t}AC=A, we find det(C)=±1\det(C)=\pm 1, so OA+​(𝐙)O_{A}^{+}(\mathbf{Z}) is the group of elements of OA+​(𝐑)O_{A}^{+}(\mathbf{R}) that have integer coefficients.

Remark 2.12

In some cases OA+​(𝐙)O_{A}^{+}(\mathbf{Z}) is very small. For example if A=(100−1)A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\ 0&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right) then OA+​(𝐙)O_{A}^{+}(\mathbf{Z}) has only two elements: (1001)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\ 0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right) and (−1001)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-1&0\\ 0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right). However, in general OA+​(𝐙)O_{A}^{+}(\mathbf{Z}) is an infinite group.

If we consider the theta functions in Definition 2.1 not only as a function of zz and τ\tau, but also as a function of c1c_{1} and c2c_{2}, we get transformation properties with respect to OA+​(𝐙)O_{A}^{+}(\mathbf{Z}):

Proposition 2.13

Let C∈OA+​(𝐙)C\in O_{A}^{+}(\mathbf{Z}), c1,c2∈C¯Qc_{1},c_{2}\in\overline{C}_{Q} and let (z,τ)∈D⁡(c1)∩D⁡(c2)(z,\tau)\in D(c_{1})\cap D(c_{2}). Let ϑAc1,c2​(z,τ)\vartheta_{A}^{c_{1},c_{2}}(z;\tau) be as in Definition 2.1. Then we have C⋅CQ=CQC\cdot C_{Q}=C_{Q}, C⋅SQ=SQC\cdot S_{Q}=S_{Q}, (C​z,τ)∈D⁡(C​c1)∩D⁡(C​c2)(Cz,\tau)\in D(Cc_{1})\cap D(Cc_{2}), and

ϑC​c1,C​c2​(C​z,τ)=ϑc1,c2​(z,τ).\vartheta^{Cc_{1},Cc_{2}}(Cz;\tau)=\vartheta^{c_{1},c_{2}}(z;\tau).
Proof.

C⋅CQ=CQC\cdot C_{Q}=C_{Q} holds by definition. If c∈𝐙rc\in\mathbf{Z}^{r} is primitive, then C​cCc is also primitive. Hence we find C⋅SQ=SQC\cdot S_{Q}=S_{Q}. We have Q⁡(C​x)=Q⁡(x)Q(Cx)=Q(x) and B⁡(C​x,C​y)=B⁡(x,y)B(Cx,Cy)=B(x,y), for all x,y∈𝐑rx,y\in\mathbf{R}^{r} and C​𝐙r=𝐙rC\mathbf{Z}^{r}=\mathbf{Z}^{r}. We see

B⁡(c,Im⁡(z)Im⁡(τ))=B⁡(C​c,C​Im⁡(z)Im⁡(τ))=B⁡(C​c,Im⁡(C​z)Im⁡(τ)).B\Bigl(c,\frac{\operatorname{Im}(z)}{\operatorname{Im}(\tau)}\Bigr)=B\Bigl(Cc,C\frac{\operatorname{Im}(z)}{\operatorname{Im}(\tau)}\Bigr)=B\Bigl(Cc,\frac{\operatorname{Im}(Cz)}{\operatorname{Im}(\tau)}\Bigr).

Hence if (z,τ)∈D⁡(c)(z,\tau)\in D(c) then (C​z,τ)∈D⁡(C​c)(Cz,\tau)\in D(Cc).

If we replace (c1,c2,z,n)(c_{1},c_{2},z,n) by (C​c1,C​c2,C​z,C​n)(Cc_{1},Cc_{2},Cz,Cn) in the definition of ϑ\vartheta we get the desired transformation property. ∎

Remark 2.14

The CC acts on both c1c_{1} and c2c_{2} at the same time.

Corollary 2.15

Let C∈OA+​(𝐙)C\in O_{A}^{+}(\mathbf{Z}), c1,c2∈C¯Qc_{1},c_{2}\in\overline{C}_{Q} and let a∈R⁡(c1)∩R⁡(c2)a\in R(c_{1})\cap R(c_{2}). Let ϑa,bc1,c2​(τ)\vartheta_{a,b}^{c_{1},c_{2}}(\tau) be as in Definition 2.1. Then

ϑC​a,C​bC​c1,C​c2​(τ)=ϑa,bc1,c2​(τ).\vartheta_{Ca,Cb}^{Cc_{1},Cc_{2}}(\tau)=\vartheta_{a,b}^{c_{1},c_{2}}(\tau).

We see that ϑa,b\vartheta_{a,b} is a holomorphic modular form of weight 1, with the same transformation properties as η2\eta^{2}. Hence ϑa,b\vartheta_{a,b} is a multiple of η2\eta^{2}. By comparing the first Fourier coefficients we find

ϑa,b=−4​eπ​i3​η2,\vartheta_{a,b}=-4e^{\frac{\pi i}{3}}\eta^{2},

or equivalently

∑n≥2​|m|(−1)n+m​q12​n2−32​m2+12​n+12​m=(q)∞2.\sum_{n\geq 2|m|}(-1)^{n+m}q^{\frac{1}{2}n^{2}-\frac{3}{2}m^{2}+\frac{1}{2}n+\frac{1}{2}m}=(q)_{\infty}^{2}.

This last equation is proven in [1, pp. 451], using different techniques. In that article several similar results are proven. The modular transformation properties of the functions involved can be found using the same method as in the examples presented here.

These examples are very special: in general, ϑa,b\vartheta_{a,b} is not a holomorphic function. However, for the special values of c1c_{1}, c2c_{2}, aa and bb given here, ϑa,b\vartheta_{a,b} is holomorphic.

In [20] a theorem about the modularity of a certain family of qq-series associated with indefinite binary quadratic forms is given. This result may also be found using the same method as in the examples presented here.

In the next two chapters, we will see some other examples. In these examples, the ϑ\vartheta-functions are not holomorphic.

Chapter 3 Fourier Coefficients of Meromorphic Jacobi Forms

11 Introduction

In this chapter we consider functions φ:𝐂×ℋ⟶𝐂\varphi:\mathbf{C}\times\mathcal{H}\longrightarrow\mathbf{C} that satisfy

φ⁡(z+λ​τ+μ,τ)=e−2​π​i​m​(λ2​τ+2​λ​z)​φ​(z,τ)∀λ,μ∈𝐙\varphi(z+\lambda\tau+\mu;\tau)=e^{-2\pi im(\lambda^{2}\tau+2\lambda z)}\varphi(z;\tau)\qquad\forall\lambda,\mu\in\mathbf{Z} (E)

and

φ⁡(zc​τ+d,a​τ+bc​τ+d)=(c​τ+d)k​e2​π​i​m​c​z2/(c​τ+d)​φ​(z,τ)∀(abcd)∈SL2⁡(𝐙),\varphi\left(\frac{z}{c\tau+d};\frac{a\tau+b}{c\tau+d}\right)=(c\tau+d)^{k}e^{2\pi imcz^{2}/(c\tau+d)}\varphi(z;\tau)\qquad\forall\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbf{Z}), (M)

with k∈𝐙k\in\mathbf{Z} and m∈𝐙>0m\in\mathbf{Z}_{>0}. The first equation gives the transformation law with respect to z↦z+λ​τ+μz\mapsto z+\lambda\tau+\mu and will be denoted by (E), for elliptic. The second equation gives the transformation law with respect to SL2⁡(𝐙)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbf{Z}) and will be denoted by (M), for modular. Jacobi forms of weight kk and index mm satisfy both (E) and (M).

It is a classical result, see [9, pp. 57–59], that the space of Jacobi forms of weight kk and index mm is isomorphic to a certain space of (vector-valued) modular forms of weight k−12k-\frac{1}{2} in one variable:

Theorem 3.1

If φ\varphi is holomorphic as a function of zz and satisfies (E), we have

φ⁡(z,τ)=∑l​mod⁡2​mhl​(τ)​ϑm,l​(z,τ),\varphi(z;\tau)=\sum_{l\operatorname{mod}2m}h_{l}(\tau)\vartheta_{m,l}(z;\tau), (48)

with Fourier coefficients

hl(τ)=e−πil2τ/2m∫pp+1φ(z;τ)e−2​π​i​l​zdzp∈𝐂h_{l}(\tau)=e^{-\pi il^{2}\tau/2m}\int_{p}^{p+1}\varphi(z;\tau)e^{-2\pi ilz}dz\qquad p\in\mathbf{C}

and

ϑm,l​(z,τ)=∑λ∈𝐙λ≡lmod2m​eπ​i​λ2​τ/2​m+2​π​i​λ​z.\vartheta_{m,l}(z;\tau)=\underset{\lambda\equiv l\operatorname{mod}2m}{\sum_{\lambda\in\mathbf{Z}}}e^{\pi i\lambda^{2}\tau/2m+2\pi i\lambda z}. (49)

If φ\varphi also satisfies the transformation (M), then we have for each ll:

hl(τ+1)=e−πil2/2mhl(τ)h_{l}(\tau+1)=e^{-\pi il^{2}/2m}h_{l}(\tau) (50)

and

hl​(−1τ)=τk−i​τ​12​m​∑ν​mod⁡2​meπ​i​l​ν/m​hν​(τ).h_{l}\Bigl(-\frac{1}{\tau}\Bigr)=\frac{\tau^{k}}{\sqrt{-i\tau}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2m}}\sum_{\nu\operatorname{mod}2m}e^{\pi il\nu/m}h_{\nu}(\tau). (51)
Proof.

If we take λ=0\lambda=0 and μ=1\mu=1 in (E) we see that φ\varphi is 1-periodic. Hence we can write

φ⁡(z,τ)=∑r∈𝐙hr​(τ)​eπ​i​r2​τ/2​m+2​π​i​r​z,\varphi(z;\tau)=\sum_{r\in\mathbf{Z}}h_{r}(\tau)e^{\pi ir^{2}\tau/2m+2\pi irz}, (52)

with

hr(τ)=e−πir2τ/2m∫pp+1φ(z;τ)e−2​π​i​r​zdzp∈𝐂.h_{r}(\tau)=e^{-\pi ir^{2}\tau/2m}\int_{p}^{p+1}\varphi(z;\tau)e^{-2\pi irz}dz\qquad p\in\mathbf{C}.

(The extra factor eπ​i​r2​τ/2​me^{\pi ir^{2}\tau/2m} in the Fourier coefficients is for convenience).

If we use (E) with λ=1\lambda=1 and μ=0\mu=0 we see that hr+2​m=hrh_{r+2m}=h_{r}. Hence hrh_{r} depends only on r​mod⁡2​mr\operatorname{mod}2m. Putting this into (52) gives

φ⁡(z,τ)=∑r∈𝐙hr​(τ)​eπ​i​r2​τ/2​m+2​π​i​r​z=∑l​mod⁡2​m∑λ∈𝐙λ≡lmod2m​hλ​(τ)​eπ​i​λ2​τ/2​m+2​π​i​λ​z=∑l​mod⁡2​mhl​(τ)​ϑm,l​(z,τ),\begin{split}\varphi(z;\tau)&=\sum_{r\in\mathbf{Z}}h_{r}(\tau)e^{\pi ir^{2}\tau/2m+2\pi irz}=\sum_{l\operatorname{mod}2m}\underset{\lambda\equiv l\operatorname{mod}2m}{\sum_{\lambda\in\mathbf{Z}}}h_{\lambda}(\tau)e^{\pi i\lambda^{2}\tau/2m+2\pi i\lambda z}\\ &=\sum_{l\operatorname{mod}2m}h_{l}(\tau)\vartheta_{m,l}(z;\tau),\end{split}

with ϑm,l\vartheta_{m,l} as in (49).

If φ\varphi also satisfies the transformation (M), then we get the transformation properties (50) and (51) of hlh_{l} from the transformation properties of ϑm,l\vartheta_{m,l} and the decomposition given in (48); see [9, pp. 58–59] for details. ∎

The hlh_{l} are more or less the Fourier coefficients of φ\varphi, if we consider φ\varphi as a function of zz. These Fourier coefficients form a vector-valued modular form.

In [3] Andrews gives most of the fifth order mock theta functions as Fourier coefficients of meromorphic Jacobi forms (i.e. meromorphic as a function of zz), namely certain quotients of ordinary Jacobi theta-series. In this chapter (see Theorem 3.9), we generalize Theorem 3.1 to include meromorphic Jacobi forms. We give the result only for Jacobi forms on the full Jacobi group (i.e. satisfying (E) and (M) without any congruence restrictions on (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu) or (abcd)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)), but it could certainly be generalized to congruence subgroups (and vector-valued Jacobi forms) and could then be combined with Andrews’s identities to obtain information about the modular properties of the fifth order mock theta functions. We will not carry this out, since the same results will be obtained in Chapter 4 using instead the results on indefinite ϑ\vartheta-functions from Chapter 2.

Definition 3.4

Let φ\varphi and du​(τ)d_{u}(\tau) be as in Corollary 3.10 and suppose that the pole uu of φ(⋅;τ)\varphi(\cdot;\tau) is of the form u=α​τ+βu=\alpha\tau+\beta, with α,β∈𝐐\alpha,\beta\in\mathbf{Q} independent of τ\tau. Chapter 4 Mock ϑ\vartheta-functions

16 Introduction

Mock ϑ\vartheta-functions were introduced by S. Ramanujan in the last letter he wrote to G.H. Hardy, dated January, 1920. For a photocopy of the mathematical part of this letter see [21, pp. 127–131] (also reproduced in [4]). In this letter, Ramanujan provided a list of 17 mock ϑ\vartheta-functions, together with identities they satisfy. Ramanujan divided his list of functions into “third order”, “fifth order” and “seventh order” functions, but did not say what he meant. There’s still no formal definition of “order”, but known identities for these mock ϑ\vartheta-functions make it clear that they are related to the numbers 3, 5 and 7. Therefore we regard the order of a mock ϑ\vartheta-function merely as a convenient label, which may or may not have a deeper significance.

In his letter, Ramanujan explained what he meant by a mock ϑ\vartheta-function. In [5] we find a formal definition. Slightly rephrased it reads: a mock ϑ\vartheta-function is a function ff of the complex variable qq, defined by a qq-series of a particular type (Ramanujan calls this the Eulerian form), which converges for |q|<1|q|<1 and satisfies the following conditions:

  • (1)

    infinitely many roots of unity are exponential singularities,

  • (2)

    for every root of unity ξ\xi there is a ϑ\vartheta-function ϑξ​(q)\vartheta_{\xi}(q) such that the difference f​(q)−ϑξ​(q)f(q)-\vartheta_{\xi}(q) is bounded as q→ξq\rightarrow\xi radially (presumably with only finitely many of the ϑξ\vartheta_{\xi} being different),

  • (3)

    there is no ϑ\vartheta-function that works for all ξ\xi, i.e. ff is not the sum of two functions, one of which is a ϑ\vartheta-function and the other a function which is bounded in all roots of unity.

(When Ramanujan refers to ϑ\vartheta-functions, he means sums, products, and quotients of series of the form ∑n∈𝐙ϵn​qa​n2+b​n\sum_{n\in\mathbf{Z}}\epsilon^{n}q^{an^{2}+bn} with a,b∈𝐐a,b\in\mathbf{Q} and ϵ=−1,1\epsilon=-1,1).

The 17 functions given by Ramanujan indeed satisfy conditions (1) and (2) (see [26], [27] and [23]). However no proof has ever been given that they also satisfy condition (3). Watson (see [26]) proved a very weak form of condition (3) for the “third order” mock ϑ\vartheta-functions, namely, that they are not equal to ϑ\vartheta-functions.

In this chapter we will see that condition (3) is not satisfied if we strengthen it slightly. Indeed, we shall discuss vector-valued mock ϑ\vartheta-functions FF for which there is a vector-valued real-analytic modular form HH such that F−HF-H is bounded in all roots of unity.

There are several ways to get these results: For example let us consider the “fifth order” mock ϑ\vartheta-function (using Watson’s notation)

f0​(q)=∑n=0∞qn2(−q,q)n,f_{0}(q)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{q^{n^{2}}}{(-q;q)_{n}},

with (a)n=(a;q)n:=(1−a)(1−aq)⋯(1−aqn−1)(a)_{n}=(a;q)_{n}:=(1-a)(1-aq)\cdots(1-aq^{n-1}). Andrews (see [2]) showed that

f0​(q)=1(q)∞​∑n≥0∑|j|≤n(−1)j​q52​n2+12​n−j2​(1−q4​n+2),f_{0}(q)=\frac{1}{(q)_{\infty}}\sum_{n\geq 0}\sum_{|j|\leq n}(-1)^{j}q^{\frac{5}{2}n^{2}+\frac{1}{2}n-j^{2}}(1-q^{4n+2}), (57)

with (q)∞=∏n=1∞(1−qn)(q)_{\infty}=\prod_{n=1}^{\infty}(1-q^{n}). Using this identity, Andrews (see [3]) showed that f0​(q)f_{0}(q) can be seen as a Fourier coefficient of a certain quotient of Jacobi theta functions. Next Hickerson (see [13]) showed that f0​(q)f_{0}(q) can be related to a sum similar to the Lerch sum discussed in Chapter I. Similar results have been found for most other mock ϑ\vartheta-functions. Hence we can extend the results of Chapter I to include these “Lerch-like” sums and thereby get the transformation properties of f0f_{0}. We may also use the techniques from Chapter 3 and the representation of the mock ϑ\vartheta-functions as a Fourier coefficient of a meromorphic Jacobi form, to find the transformation properties. However, we will use (57) and similar identities for the other mock ϑ\vartheta-functions and apply the results from Chapter 2.

17 General results

Before we start with the mock ϑ\vartheta-functions, we derive some general results, which we will use repeatedly.

Definition 4.1

For a,b∈𝐑a,b\in\mathbf{R} and τ∈ℋ\tau\in\mathcal{H} we define

Ra,b​(τ)=∑ν∈a+𝐙sgn⁡(ν)​β​(2​ν2​y)​e−π​i​ν2​τ−2​π​i​ν​b,R_{a,b}(\tau)=\sum_{\nu\in a+\mathbf{Z}}\operatorname{sgn}(\nu)\beta(2\nu^{2}y)\ e^{-\pi i\nu^{2}\tau-2\pi i\nu b},

    ∂∂τ¯​Ra,b​(τ)=−i​12​y​ga,−b​(−τ¯)\frac{\partial}{\partial\overline{\tau}}R_{a,b}(\tau)=-i\frac{1}{\sqrt{2y}}\ g_{a,-b}(-\overline{\tau}).

20 Other mock ϑ\vartheta-functions

In the previous sections we have dealt with the seventh order and most of the fifth order mock ϑ\vartheta-functions from Ramanujan’s letter. We were able to do this because identities for these mock ϑ\vartheta-functions were available in the literature. Similar identities for the other two fifth order mock ϑ\vartheta-functions, χ0\chi_{0} and χ1\chi_{1}, are not available in the literature, as far as I know. I have found the following identities (which I will not prove here) for χ0\chi_{0} and χ1\chi_{1}

χ0​(q)=2−1(q)∞2(∑k,l,m≥0+∑k,l,m<0)(−1)k+l+mq12​k2+12​l2+12​m2+2​k​l+2​k​m+2​l​m+12​(k+l+m),χ1​(q)=1(q)∞2(∑k,l,m≥0+∑k,l,m<0)(−1)k+l+mq12​k2+12​l2+12​m2+2​k​l+2​k​m+2​l​m+32​(k+l+m).\begin{split}\chi_{0}(q)&=2-\frac{1}{(q)_{\infty}^{2}}\Bigl(\sum_{k,l,m\geq 0}+\sum_{k,l,m<0}\Bigr)(-1)^{k+l+m}q^{\frac{1}{2}k^{2}+\frac{1}{2}l^{2}+\frac{1}{2}m^{2}+2kl+2km+2lm+\frac{1}{2}(k+l+m)},\\ \chi_{1}(q)&=\frac{1}{(q)_{\infty}^{2}}\Bigl(\sum_{k,l,m\geq 0}+\sum_{k,l,m<0}\Bigr)(-1)^{k+l+m}q^{\frac{1}{2}k^{2}+\frac{1}{2}l^{2}+\frac{1}{2}m^{2}+2kl+2km+2lm+\frac{3}{2}(k+l+m)}.\end{split}

These series are similar to the ones we used for the seventh and fifth order mock theta functions. However, the quadratic form is of type (1,2)(1,2). Hence we cannot apply any of the results from Chapter 2. However, in [27] identities for χ0\chi_{0} and χ1\chi_{1} are given which give χ0\chi_{0} and χ1\chi_{1} as a linear combination of other fifth order mock ϑ\vartheta-functions. Hence, we could derive the transformation properties of χ0\chi_{0} and χ1\chi_{1}.

In Ramanujan’s letter four third order mock ϑ\vartheta-functions are given. Watson (see [26]) defined three more third order mock ϑ\vartheta-functions. Later even more exotic mock ϑ\vartheta-functions were introduced: of sixth order (see [5]), of eighth order (see [10]) and of tenth order (see [6], [7] and [8]). In these articles, identities are given, which relate the mock ϑ\vartheta-functions to sums of the same type as the ones we used for the fifth and seventh order mock ϑ\vartheta-functions. Hence, using the same techniques, we could derive the transformation properties of these mock ϑ\vartheta-functions. In [30] I derive the transformation properties of the vector-valued third order mock ϑ\vartheta-function

F⁡(τ)=(q−124​f​(q)2​q13​ω​(q12)2​q13​ω​(−q12)).F(\tau)=\begin{pmatrix}q^{-\frac{1}{24}}f(q)\\ 2q^{\frac{1}{3}}\omega(q^{\frac{1}{2}})\\ 2q^{\frac{1}{3}}\omega(-q^{\frac{1}{2}})\end{pmatrix}.

The result is similar to the results found in this chapter. \clearemptydoublepage

Samenvatting

Dit proefschrift gaat over mock thetafuncties. Deze mock thetafuncties zijn een “uitvinding” van de Indiase wiskundige Srinivasa Ramanujan. Ramanujan leefde van 1887 tot 1920. Hoewel hij nooit een universitaire studie heeft afgemaakt, wordt hij door velen gezien als een wiskundig genie. Ramanujan werkte erg intuïtief en bewees zelden z’n beweringen. Dit komt doordat hij door z’n onvolledige wiskundige opleiding nooit de kunst van het bewijzen heeft aangeleerd. Het leven en werk van Ramanujan bevat dan ook een element van mysterie en romantiek.

De mock thetafuncties ontdekte Ramanujan kort voor hij op 32 jarige leeftijd stierf. Hoewel verschillende wiskundigen zich na de dood van Ramanujan met de mock thetafuncties hebben beziggehouden, en ook verschillende resultaten hebben geboekt, is nooit echt duidelijk geworden wat er nu werkelijk aan de hand is. Daardoor vormen ze nog steeds een bron van raadsels voor hedendaagse wiskundigen. In dit proefschrift plaats ik de voorbeelden die Ramanujan gaf van mock thetafuncties in een diepere achterliggende theorie (namelijk die van reëel analytische modulaire vormen). Hiermee kan een natuurlijke verklaring worden gegeven voor de eigenschappen van mock thetafuncties, zoals Ramanujan die beschreef.

Het engelse werkwoord “to mock” betekent overigens zoiets als bespotten of spottend naäpen. We zouden dus ook kunnen spreken over spottende thetafuncties of nepthetafuncties (thetafuncties waren in Ramanujans tijd reeds uitgebreid bestudeerd en ook Ramanujan was hier vertrouwd mee), maar dit dekt niet helemaal de lading. In “Alice in Wonderland” van Lewis Carroll komt een nepschildpad (mock turtle) voor. Hiervan wordt nepschildpadsoep (mock turtle soup) gemaakt. In werkelijkheid is nepschildpadsoep natuurlijk nagemaakte schildpadsoep (gemaakt van kalfshoofd, kalfsvlees, etc.)

In hoofdstuk 1 bekijk ik de som

∑n∈𝐙(−1)n​eπ​i​(n2+n)​τ+2​π​i​n​v1−e2​π​i​n​τ+2​π​i​u(τ∈ℋ,v∈𝐂,u∈𝐂∖(𝐙​τ+𝐙)).\sum_{n\in\mathbf{Z}}\frac{(-1)^{n}e^{\pi i(n^{2}+n)\tau+2\pi inv}}{1-e^{2\pi in\tau+2\pi iu}}\qquad(\tau\in\mathcal{H},v\in\mathbf{C},u\in\mathbf{C}\setminus(\mathbf{Z}\tau+\mathbf{Z})).

Ik noem dit een Lerch som, omdat deze som ook al werd bestudeerd door Lerch. Deze Lerch som transformeert bijna als een Jacobivorm onder substituties in (u,v,τ)(u,v,\tau). Ik laat zien dat het transformatiegedrag precies dat van een Jacobivorm wordt als we er een (relatief eenvoudige) correctieterm bij optellen. Deze correctieterm blijkt niet holomorf te zijn in (u,v,τ)(u,v,\tau), alleen reëel analytisch. Voor bepaalde waarden van (u,v)(u,v) zouden we de Lerch som als functie van τ\tau een mock thetafunctie kunnen noemen, hoewel deze niet expliciet bij Ramanujan voorkomen.

In hoofdstuk 2 bekijk ik thetafuncties bij indefiniete kwadratische vormen. Deze thetafuncties zijn een aanpassing van een klasse van thetafuncties geïntroduceerd door Göttsche en Zagier, en lijken op de thetafuncties ingevoerd door Siegel. Voor deze indefiniete thetafuncties vind ik elliptisch en modulair transformatiegedrag, analoog aan het transformatiegedrag van thetafuncties behorende bij positief definiete kwadratische vormen. In het geval van positief definiete kwadratische vormen zijn de thetafuncties holomorf. De thetafuncties in dit hoofdstuk zijn dat niet. Door specialisatie van de parameters is het mogelijk om mock thetafuncties te verkrijgen uit deze indefiniete thetafuncties.

In hoofdstuk 3 bestudeer ik de modulariteit van de Fourier coëfficiënten van meromorfe Jacobivormen.

In hoofdstuk 4 gebruik ik het verband tussen mock thetafuncties en de indefiniete thetafuncties uit hoofdstuk 2, om deze mock thetafuncties in verband te brengen met reëel analytische modulaire vormen. We hadden echter even goed de methoden uit hoofdstuk 1 of hoofdstuk 3 kunnen gebruiken om tot hetzelfde resultaat te komen. Niet alle mock thetafuncties vallen in dit kader: Voor een tweetal mock thetafuncties van orde 5 zou een uitbreiding van mijn theorie gewenst zijn tot een andere klasse van indefiniete kwadratische vormen.

Dankwoord

Op deze plaats wil ik een aantal mensen noemen die een rol hebben gespeeld bij het tot stand komen van dit proefschrift.

Allereerst ben ik veel dank verschuldigd aan Don Zagier en Roelof Bruggeman, mijn promotoren en begeleiders. Don: hoewel onze gesprekken niet erg veelvuldig waren, waren ze altijd erg stimulerend en inspirerend. De belangrijkste ideeën in dit proefschrift zijn dan ook uit deze gesprekken voortgekomen. Verder ben ik je veel dank verschuldigd voor het helpen bij het (enigszins) leesbaar maken van m’n proefschrift. Roelof: het was erg fijn om iemand te hebben om wekelijks de zaken door te spreken. Zeker in de eindfase, omdat je iedere keer weer bereid was om commentaar te leveren op hetgeen ik geschreven had. Hoewel ik je in het begin misschien iets te precies vond, ben ik je daar achteraf alleen maar dankbaar voor.

I would like to thank my thesis examiners Bruce Berndt, Hans Duistermaat, Joop Kolk and Loïc Merel, for reading the manuscript.

Verder ben ik m’n ouders dankbaar voor hun voortdurende belangstelling en hun vertrouwen.

Tenslotte bedank ik Therese, voor alles.

Curriculum Vitae

Sander Zwegers is op 16 april 1975 geboren te Oosterhout (N.B.). Hij groeide op in ’s Gravenmoer en haalde in 1993 het VWO-diploma aan het Dr. Schaepmancollege te Dongen. Hierna ging hij studeren aan de Universiteit Utrecht, en in augustus 1994 haalde hij zijn propedeuse Wiskunde (cum laude) en Natuurkunde (cum laude). In augustus 1998 studeerde hij af in de Wiskunde (cum laude) bij Dr. J.A.C. Kolk, met de scriptie “Theta functions, certain modular forms arising from them and Rogers–Ramanujan type identities”. Tijdens zijn studie was Sander lid van de faculteitsraad van de Faculteit Wiskunde en Informatica, gaf hij als studentassistent werkcolleges en vervulde hij diverse functies bij de studievereniging A-Eskwadraat, waaronder het voorzitterschap.

Vanaf oktober 1998 was hij werkzaam als assistent in opleiding (AiO) bij het Mathematisch Instituut van de faculteit Wiskunde en Informatica van de Universiteit Utrecht, met Prof. dr. D.B. Zagier als promotor, en Dr. R.W. Bruggeman als copromotor. Het onderzoek dat hij daar deed heeft geresulteerd in dit proefschrift. In het kader van zijn onderzoek heeft hij voordrachten geven op enkele conferenties en instituten: in Urbana-Champaign (VS), Bonn (Duitsland) en Luminy (Frankrijk). Daarnaast gaf hij onderwijs, was hij lid van de faculteitsraad van de Faculteit Wiskunde en Informatica en was hij lid van de benoemingsadviescommissie algebra.

Vanaf 1 januari 2003 zal hij voor één jaar als postdoc aan het Max-Planck-Institut für Mathematik (Bonn) verbonden zijn.
